results.why: Deck B is a coherent Jeskai control deck with consistent mana: Lute ramps into Jeskai Revelation, and it has clean removal (Get Lost, Helix, Traumatic Critique) and counters (No More Lies, Three Steps Ahead). Deck A tries to be four colors, with Inevitable Defeat needing R, W and B alongside Tablet, Flashback and a lone North Wind Avatar. That makes its mana greedy, and a pile of one-ofs and tapped lands makes its card choices look scattered. Deck B's Inevitable Defeat is also a stretch for its mana, but its base is far more focused.

Deck A has a cleaner, stronger core: 4 Lightning Helix, 4 No More Lies, 3 Get Lost, Three Steps Ahead and Day of Judgment, with card flow from Consult the Star Charts and Stock Up. Resonating Lute fits its instant/sorcery plan and helps cast Jeskai Revelation. Black is thin for 4 Inevitable Defeat, but Deck B has the same problem and also runs weak or clunky cards like Flashback, a lone North Wind Avatar, Tablet of Discovery and Mistrise Village.

Deck B has a coherent ramp-into-Nature's-Rhythm plan with Llanowar Elves, Bloom Tender and Spider Manifestation fetching Craterhoof and Ouroboroid, and it has the red sources to cast The Jolly Balloon Man. Deck A is a four-color pile with very little synergy: it runs only 1 Plains for white, uses The Jolly Balloon Man with no red source at all, and has Brightglass Gearhulk with only a handful of 1-drop targets. Deck B's mana has some strain, but it is far more functional than Deck A's.

Deck A has a clear plan: mana dorks ramp into Nature's Rhythm, Craterhoof, Ouroboroid and Brightglass Gearhulk, with Gearhulk fetching cheap creatures and artifacts. Its mana is greedy because it splashes red and blue, but Temple Garden, Verge and Multiversal Passage make it workable. Deck B is a pile of unrelated cards: Stormchaser's Talent with almost no spells to use it on, a lone Jolly Balloon Man with no red source, and Nature's Rhythm with few worthwhile targets.

Deck B has a coherent Dwarf-equipment plan with real interaction (Burst Lightning, Shock, Mjölnir), a sensible 24-land mana base, and efficient equipment like Jitte and Mattock. Deck A is clunky: it runs 60 cards with 8+ expensive or weak equipment (Doc Ock's Tentacles, Leyline Axe, Dragonfire Blade), no removal, a 1-of Basilisk Collar and Multiversal Passage, and a worse creature count with off-theme filler. B's curve, burn, and legendary Dwarf core make it far more tournament-ready.

Deck A has a focused, coherent dwarf-equipment plan: cheap Dwarves (Mauler, Kíli, Dáin's Company, Giott), efficient equipment (Jitte, Mattock, Spider-Suit, Mjölnir), and eight burn spells to interact. Its mana is solid with 23 lands in a two-color deck. Deck B has too many clunky equipment (Doc Ock's Tentacles, Leyline Axe at 4 mana, Basilisk Collar, Dragonfire Blade), no removal besides Thorin, and a weak creature count for that many equipment pieces, so it is less consistent.

Deck B is a focused mono-black sacrifice and recursion deck with a cheap curve, Bloodghast and Forsaken Miner as recursive fodder, Popular Egotist and Rat King as payoffs, and clean removal, and its mana is consistent with 22 black sources. Deck A is a greedy three-color pile with a thin red splash for Biotech Specialist and Mutagen Man, many tapped lands, and Gene Pollinator that is awkward to use; its Rottenmouth Viper finisher is also clunky. Deck B has some weaknesses, such as Forsaken Miner and Bloodghast being unable to block, but it is far more coherent and consistent.

Deck A is a focused mono-black aggro-sacrifice deck with cheap recursive threats (Bloodghast, Forsaken Miner, Nine-Lives Familiar), sac outlets and drain payoffs, and its mana is clean with 22 lands that nearly all make black. Deck B is a greedy three-color mess: it has many ETB-tapped lands, off-color cards like Biotech Specialist and Mutagen Man that need red or green, only 1 Mutagen Man, and a clunky 6-drop Viper, so its mana and plan are much less consistent.

Deck B is a coherent, low-curve Boros planeswalker-control deck with cheap interaction (Burst Lightning, Helix, Get Lost, Sear), Voice of Victory as an early play, and a clean 24-land base of dual lands and basics. Deck A is a pile of conflicting ideas: Day of Judgment alongside token makers, weak cards like Way of the Pyromancer and Aang's Iceberg, Erode giving the opponent lands, and a clunky mana base with colorless Fountainports and slow lands.

Deck A is a coherent, consistent Boros walker deck: a clean mana base with 24 lands, a low curve of Voice of Victory and cheap removal, and planeswalkers that Gideon's Memorial helps cast. Deck B is a clunky pile: Way of the Pyromancer and Caretaker's Talent lack enough token support, Day of Judgment fights its own creature and token plan, and colorless lands like Fountainport and Sunken Citadel strain a deck with RR and WW costs.

Deck B has a more coherent, consistent plan: 8 mana elves plus Badgermole Cub, then Ouroboroid, Fight Rigging, Great Henge and Kiora as payoffs, and Craterhoof and Ghalta as finishers. It also has a clean 60 cards with a sensible land package (Boseiju, Lair, Nykthos). Deck A runs 63 cards, and its Emrakul, Summon: Bahamut and Titan of Industry are clunky, so its top end is less cohesive.

Deck A has a more coherent and consistent plan: 8 mana elves plus Badgermole Cub ramp into Ouroboroid, Great Henge, Kiora and Fight Rigging, with Craterhoof and Ghalta as finishers and Boseiju as free utility. Deck B is clunkier, with Emrakul, Summon: Bahamut and Titan of Industry that are hard to cast or poor fits, and 4 Nykthos with little devotion is risky. Deck B's Ba Sing Se and Spider Manifestation are fine, but its top end is less reliable and its mana is worse.

Deck B is a coherent mono-white heroic deck with 18 creatures, cheap targeting spells and protection to back them up. Its mana is perfect, with Mutavault and Eiganjo adding utility and Phalanx Leader's WW cost causing no trouble. Deck A is a messy Boros build with weak red cards like Academic Dispute and Reckless Rage, plus Mana Confluence life loss and a stretched mana base for little gain.

Deck A is a focused mono-white heroic deck with 18 creatures, a good set of cheap targeting spells, and clean mana with Mutavault and Eiganjo. Deck B splits into two colors and plays weak cards like Academic Dispute, Reckless Rage, and Speedball, with only 14 creatures to carry the targeting spells. Its mana is also strained by Mana Confluence and painlands, and it loses Phalanx Leader and the best protection spells.

Deck B is a coherent Jeskai control shell: cheap interaction (Helix, Sear, Get Lost, No More Lies), sweepers, and Wandering Emperor, backed by many tri-lands and dual lands that support three colors. Deck A is weaker: it runs only 2 Fiery Impulse-style cheap interaction beyond its core, has 4 Inevitable Defeat requiring black with few black sources (Godless Shrine, two Shattered Sanctum, Gloomlake Verge), and includes clunky cards like Together as One and Erode. Its mana of tapped and conditional lands is also awkward, while B's mana is smoother and its Inevitable Defeat count is more restrained.

Deck A has a fuller interaction suite for the Jeskai Revelation shell: No More Lies, Get Lost, Sear, Supreme Verdict and The Wandering Emperor, alongside Helix and Inevitable Defeat. Its mana is a patchwork of single-copy lands but covers W, U, R and B well, with six dedicated black sources plus Great Hall for Inevitable Defeat. Deck B leans on weaker cards like Together as One, Erode (which ramps the opponent) and Farewell (which exiles its own Tablets), and it has no counterspells.

Deck B is a coherent Izzet spells deck. Its cheap cantrips and burn fill the graveyard and cheapen Tolarian Terror and Eddymurk Crab, and the burn and counters give it real interaction. Deck A is a slower durdle pile of bounce and card selection with few threats and little interaction, and 4 Stormchaser's Talent plus the Terrors and Crabs is not enough to win consistently. Deck B's green splash for Bushwhack is a little greedy, but the mana is still much better than A's.

Deck A is a coherent Izzet/Simic spells shell with cheap cantrips and burn that fill the graveyard, which makes Tolarian Terror and Eddymurk Crab cheap, and it has real interaction (Fiery Impulse, Burst Lightning, Lightning Axe). Its mana has plenty of duals, though three colors with Bushwhack and several green lands is a bit greedy. Deck B has only 8 or so instants and sorceries, so the Terror and Crab discounts barely work, and its Cache Grab, Up the Beanstalk and bounce suite is slow and doesn't pressure or answer anything.

Deck B is a coherent Modern Archon reanimator list: it fills the graveyard with Supplier, Looting and Eyetwitch, then reanimates with Persist, backed by cheap interaction (Push, Bolt, Bowmasters) and a real mana base. Deck A is a pile of mostly clunky cards with 4 Street Wraith, 4 Overlord and Troll, odd lands such as Phyrexian Tower and Crypt of Agadeem, and only 4 Persist. It lacks the consistency to cast or reanimate its payoffs efficiently, and its mana is awkward.

Deck A has a clear plan: Stitcher's Supplier, Faithless Looting and Eyetwitch fill the graveyard, while Bloodghast and Persist bring back Archon of Cruelty. Cheap removal (Push, Bolt, Flare) and the Phoenix backup give it a lot of interaction, and the Blood Crypt, fetch and Raucous Theater mana supports the light red splash. Deck B is clunkier, with five-mana Street Wraith and Troll, a stray Poet's Quill, and several green-typed lands that add little. It also has less fast graveyard filling and fewer good one-drop plays.

Deck B has a coherent ramp plan: Utopia Sprawl, Halfling, Talisman and Mycospawn feed into Emrakul, Sire and Devourer. It also has 24-plus mana sources and Turntimber as a flexible spell/land. Deck A is a pile of 60 cards with 4 Emrakul, 2 Ulamog and 2 Ugin on a mana base of colorless lands that can't reliably cast its green cards, plus awkward cards like Mosswort Bridge, Gemstone Caverns and Dryad Arbor.

Deck A has a coherent ramp plan: Utopia Sprawl, Halfling, and Talisman into Eldrazi bombs, with Fight Rigging and Turntimber Symbiosis as extra threats. It runs 25 lands plus 11+ mana sources, and its Temples and Labyrinths support the colorless spells. Deck B is greedier and less consistent: Gemstone Caverns, Dryad Arbor, and Mosswort Bridge are weak in a deck with expensive bombs, it plays 10-drops and Ugin without enough early acceleration, and Green Sun's Zenith has few good targets.

Deck B is a coherent artifact-storm shell: Dark Ritual, LED, Petals and Moxen feed Infernal Tutor, Echo of Eons, Tendrils and Paradoxical Outcome, and its blue-black mana supports all of it. Deck A is incoherent, with Defense Grid hurting its own plan, too few real win conditions (one Grapeshot), and a mana base and color requirements that don't line up with Gamble, the Talents and Chrome Mox imprints.

Deck A is a coherent artifact/storm combo shell: Dark Ritual, LED, Petals and Moxen feed Infernal Tutor, Echo of Eons and Tendrils, with Thoughtseize for protection and a mana base that supports blue and black. Deck B is a muddled mix of Defense Grid, Gamble, Grapeshot, Urza's Saga and Hexing Squelcher, with no clear way to win and an unreliable mana base. Deck A's numbers are a bit odd, such as only one Tendrils, but it can still execute its plan.

Deck B is a coherent Arclight Phoenix spells deck. Mutagenic Growth, Gut Shot, Lava Dart, Bolt, Looting and the cantrips are cheap instants and sorceries that turn on Phoenix's three-spell recursion, and the 16 lands support both red and blue. Deck A mixes Daze, Thoughtseize and four Fantasticars into a Phoenix shell without enough cheap spells to make Phoenix recur reliably, and its mana is stretched across too many colors and effects.

Deck A is a focused Arclight Phoenix shell. Buried Alive and Faithless Looting put Phoenix in the graveyard, and a pile of cheap instants and sorceries (Ritual, Brainstorm, Ponder, Bolt, Gut Shot, Lava Dart, Growth) turns it back on. The mana is solid, with 16 lands, plenty of red and black sources, and Force of Will as protection. Deck B mixes in Daze, Thoughtseize and Fantasticar, which pull against each other, and it plays only 15 lands, including a tapped Thundering Falls and few Islands for Daze, so the plan is less coherent.

Deck B is a coherent R/W metalcraft-affinity deck with real interaction (Lightning Bolt, Galvanic Blast, Journey), good fliers and a mana base of artifact lands that supports it. Deck A is mono-white with no removal and a clunky mix of cards like Spider-Man and Leonardo; it includes 4 Ancient Den but 10 Plains and unneeded Springleaf Drums, so it is weaker and less focused.

Deck A is a coherent R/W artifact-aggro deck: artifact lands, Drum, Synthesizer and Ornithopter enable metalcraft, which powers Ardent Recruit and Galvanic Blast. It adds proven Pauper staples like Lightning Bolt, Kor Skyfisher, Glint Hawk and Journey to Nowhere, and its mana base of 13 artifact lands plus basics supports both colors. Deck B is mono-white with only 4 Ancient Den and weak or odd cards like Phyrexian Walker, Packbeast, Ramosian Rally and the unusual legends, and it lacks real removal and consistent power.

Deck B is a coherent Boros aggro-midrange deck with good removal (Bolt, Journey, Lava Dart), efficient creatures, and a mana base that fits its colors. Deck A is a confused pile: Sneaky Snacker is blue-black and uncastable on Boros lands, there are too few creatures to support its looting, and it runs 4 Escape Tunnel and a graveyard plan without real payoffs. Deck B's curve and mana are much more reliable.}</br>

Deck A is a coherent Boros aggro/midrange deck: multicolored creatures and spells that return the Eidolons, plus Bolt, Journey and Lava Dart, on a clean two-color mana base. Deck B includes Sneaky Snacker, a blue-black card it cannot cast, and Inside Out, which needs blue or red hybrid mana. Its mana is also strained by Escape Tunnel, and it runs 3 Faithless Looting and 4 Pursue the Past with few real payoffs, so its plan is incoherent.

Deck B has a coherent engine: Survival of the Fittest, Birds of Paradise and Wall of Blossoms feed Academy Rector, Karmic Guide, Deranged Hermit and Goblin Bombardment. Its fetchlands and Birds support the five colors reasonably well, even though three Future Sight needing UUU is a stretch. Deck A is a pile of four colors with an 8-mana Decree of Silence, Gaea's Blessing, and only one Forest behind a four-of green one-drop, so its mana and plan don't hang together.

Deck A is a coherent Rector/Survival creature engine. Birds and Wall of Blossoms ramp and cantrip, Survival and Rector find the top end, and Bombardment, Therapy and Phyrexian Tower give sacrifice outlets that feed Rector, Karmic Guide and Squee. Its mana is greedy across five colors, with Future Sight's UUU the worst spot, but Birds, fetchlands and painlands mostly cover it. Deck B has only 11 creatures and a scattered plan, with weak slots like Gaea's Blessing and three 8-mana Decrees.

Deck B has a coherent reanimator plan: Putrid Imp, Buried Alive and Survival put Bloodfire Colossus or Symbiotic Wurm into the graveyard, and Exhume, Reanimate, Animate Dead, Dark Ritual and Lotus Petal bring them back fast. Its mana is heavily black and fixed by City of Brass, Gemstone Mine and Sulfurous Springs. Deck A is a pile of clunky, unrelated top-end creatures (Nicol Bolas, Dragon Tyrant, Phantom Nishoba) with a shaky mana base of 2 Swamp and only 2 Mountain, and its Sneak Attack and Survival plan lacks the density to be consistent.

Deck A is a coherent reanimator shell: Buried Alive, Survival and Putrid Imp fill the graveyard, then Exhume, Reanimate and Animate Dead bring back Bloodfire Colossus for a one-sided sweep, with Dark Ritual and Cabal Therapy as support. Its mana is workable, with plenty of black sources from City of Brass, Llanowar Wastes, Swamp and Sulfurous Springs. Deck B is a clunky pile: Sneak Attack wants red but the mana has only about 14 red sources, and Nicol Bolas, Phantom Nishoba and Dragon Tyrant are poor top-ends. It also splits into black, green and red without reliable support, so A is much more consistent.
